figures.caption: Figure 1: Our stimulus optimization pipeline. (A) Our encoding model predicts activity in early visual cortex using a deep CNN backbone, constrained by a Gaussian that models voxel population receptive field (pRF). (B) Visualization of our RF-DiVE and RF-GO frameworks. In RF-DiVE, the optimization process is constrained by a diffusion model, while RF-GO optimizes the image using MACO. (C) Examples of most-exciting-images (MEIs) for individual voxels in V1, V2, V3, and hV4. Each column corresponds to one visual area; white circle labels the voxel’s pRF

Figure 2: Spatial and feature specificity of V1 MEIs. (A) Top 5 MEIs for an example voxel using both frameworks. The MEIs show consistent patterns within the pRF (white circle, 3σ range of the Gaussian) and greater variation outside it. (B) Full-image and pRF-zoomed views of an example MEI. (C–F) pRF-zoomed top 5 natural images and MEIs for four example V1 voxels, shown for both ADV-RN50 and DINO-RN50 backbones. See Appendix A.11 for more examples.

Figure 3: Feature specificity of hV4 MEIs across generation encoders. Top 5 natural images and MEIs are shown for two example hV4 voxels (A-B show the same voxel, C-D show the same voxel). Note the pRF is fit separately for each backbone and the rank number of voxels is assigned separately for each backbone. See Appendix A.11 for more examples, including from V2 and V3.

Figure 4: Predicted responses to top 10 images for S1. Top-10 ranking model-selected images for each image group were evaluated by the generation, ranking, and independent test encoders. Each point represents mean prediction across images for one voxel; horizontal bar = mean across voxels in S1. See Appendix A.6 for the other NSD subjects.

Figure 5: Predicted difference score (advantage of MEIs over LAION-fMRI) across subjects. For each voxel, we computed the predicted-response difference between MEIs and natural images. Points reflect the mean of these differences across voxels within each subject and ROI.

Figure 6: Chromatic and spatial-frequency statistics for V1 MEIs. (A) Colorfulness (Hasler & Suesstrunk, 2003) and CIELAB color statistics. (B) Normalized Gabor magnitude profiles across spatial frequencies, shown for RF-DiVE and RF-GO. Similar patterns were observed in V2, V3, and hV4.

Figure 7: Depiction of form in MEIs. Proportion of trials in which participants selected the hV4 images as having more threedimensional form than the V1 images, using pRF-zoomed images (left) or full images (right). Bar height and error bars indicate mean±SEM across 32 participants; asterisk indicates a significant difference from 0.50 (one-sample t-test; p<0.01).

Table 1: Paired-voxel tests of MEI responses against natural controls. Positive t favors MEIs; n is the paired-voxel count. Bold adjusted p values indicate significantly higher MEI responses after BH correction across all 256 comparisons. Results continue on the following pages.

Figure 16: Verification of full-image and pRF-weighted luma constraints. Each point summarizes one subject and generation backbone; horizontal bars indicate means across subjects. Statistics were averaged over images, voxels, and ROIs in sequence. Dotted lines and shaded bands indicate targets and tolerances. Measurements use saved-image resolution; subsequent encoder-input resizing can change RMS contrast.
